Set up a vector named age, consisting of 15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8.

Question #2:

rep(c("A","B"), each = 2) and rep(c("A","B"), times = 2) both produce a vector of length 4, but with different element orders.
Explain in your own words the difference between each and times.
  
  The each argument repeats each element individually before moving to the next element, while the times argument repeats the entire vector. For example, rep(c("A","B"), each = 2) produces A, A, B, B, whereas rep(c("A","B"), times = 2) produces A, B, A, B. Both vectors have a length of 4, but the order of the elements is different.


Question #3:

Compare seq(1, 20, by = 2) with seq(1, 20, length.out = 5). What does each argument (by vs length.out) control, and when would you use one over the other in a real analysis?

  The by argument controls the interval between numbers, while length.out controls the total number of values in the sequence. For example, seq(1, 20, by = 2) generates numbers from 1 to 20 with an interval of 2, while seq(1, 20, length.out = 5) generates 5 evenly spaced numbers between 1 and 20. In a real analysis, I would use by when I need a fixed interval, such as measuring data every 2 years, and length.out when I need a specific number of evenly spaced values for a graph or analysis.

Question #5:

Negative indexing (grades[-1]) removes an element, while logical indexing (grades[grades >= 85]) filters by a condition.

Describe a real situation where you would need negative indexing, and a different situation where logical indexing would be the better tool.

  Negative indexing is useful when I want to remove specific elements from a vector, such as excluding a student's grade because of a data entry mistake. Logical indexing is better when I want to select elements based on a condition, such as finding all students who received a grade of 85 or higher.


Question #6:

```{r}

grades[10]

```

What happens if you run grades[10] (an index that doesn’t exist)? Run it, observe the result, and explain why R responds this way instead of throwing an error.

  R returns NA because the vector contains only 5 elements, and the 10th element does not exist. R returns a missing value instead of an error because accessing an out-of-range position in a vector is allowed.

Question #8:

In the vectors-recycling chunk, z has 6 elements and short has only 2. R still produced an answer instead of an error.

Explain, in your own words, what R’s “recycling rule” did to short to make the addition work.

R’s recycling rule repeats the elements of the shorter vector until it matches the length of the longer vector. In this example, short becomes 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, allowing R to add it element-wise to z without an error.



Question #9: Now try adding z (length 6) to c(1, 0, 1) (length 3) instead. Does it work cleanly?

```{r}

z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)

z + c(1, 0, 1)

```

  It works cleanly because the length of z (6) is a multiple of 3, so R recycles the shorter vector twice without a warning.



Then try adding z to c(1, 0, 1, 1) (length 4). Compare the warning (or lack of one) in each case, and explain what condition determines whether R recycles silently versus with a warning.


```{r}

z + c(1, 0, 1, 1)

```

  R recycles a shorter vector silently when the longer vector's length is an exact multiple of the shorter vector's length. If it is not an exact multiple, R still performs the operation but issues a warning because some elements are reused only partially.

Question #10:

student["grades"] and student[["grades"]] look similar but return objects of different classes.

Run class() on each and explain the difference in what single-bracket [ ] versus double-bracket [[ ]] return from a list.

```{r}

class(student["grades"])
class(student[["grades"]])

```


  When I run class(student["grades"]), the result is "list" because single brackets [ ] return a sublist containing the selected element. When I run class(student[["grades"]]), the result is "numeric" because double brackets [[ ]] extract the actual grades vector from the list.


Question #11:

Why do you think R makes a distinction between [ ] and [[ ]] for lists, but a vector only needs [ ]? Think about what a list can contain that a vector cannot.

```{r}

student["grades"]
student[["grades"]]

```


  R makes a distinction between [ ] and [[ ]] for lists because a list can contain different types of objects, such as numbers, text, vectors, and other lists. Single brackets [ ] return a list containing the selected element, while double brackets [[ ]] return the element itself. A vector contains elements of the same basic type, so using [ ] is usually enough to select individual elements.

Question #12:

In challenge-1, you combined logical indexing on one vector (in_stock) to filter a different vector (item) inside the same list. Explain, step by step, why inventory$item[inventory$in_stock] works even though item and in_stock are stored as separate elements of the list.

  The expression inventory$item[inventory$in_stock] works because inventory$item contains the item names, while inventory$in_stock contains the logical values TRUE or FALSE. First, R accesses the item names from the list. Next, it checks which positions in inventory$in_stock are TRUE. Finally, it uses those same positions to select the corresponding item names. This returns only the items that are currently in stock, which are "Notebook" and "Pen".


Question #13:

Suppose a classmate stores related data as three separate, unconnected vectors (item_names, item_prices, item_stock) instead of grouping them into one list like inventory. What risks or bugs could this create as the dataset grows or gets reordered? Argue for or against using a list (or, later, a data frame) instead of separate vectors.

  Using separate, unconnected vectors can create errors as the dataset grows because the item names, prices, and stock information might become misaligned if an element is added, removed, or reordered in only one vector. For example, a product could accidentally be assigned the wrong price or stock status. I would recommend grouping related data in a list or, preferably, a data frame because they keep related information organized. A data frame is especially useful because each row represents one product and its corresponding details, making the data easier to manage, filter, and analyze.


----------------------------------------------

CONCLUSION.

In 3–4 sentences, summarize the key differences between vectors and lists in R, and explain when you would choose one data structure over the other.

  Vectors in R store elements of the same basic data type, while lists can store different types of data, such as numbers, text, logical values, and other vectors. Vectors are useful for performing mathematical calculations, filtering data, and working with a collection of similar values. Lists are better when I need to group different types of related information, such as a student's name, age, and grades. I would choose a vector for simple, similar data and a list when I need to organize different kinds of information together.
